To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

senescent cells secrete a large number of factors associated with inflammation, malignancy and aging, and that the p53 tumor-suppressor and the oncogene Ras regulate the secretory phenotype of senescent cells in a manner that can affect cancer development.
senescent cells secrete factors that can promote malignancy, and that oncogenic Ras and p53 can influence this process.

genotoxic stress induced cellular senescence causes cells to secrete a myriad of factors that promote inflammation and malignancy and that this senescence associated secretion phenotype (SASP), in turn, can promote malignancy in a cell nonautonomic manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which normal cells are transformed into cancer cells.
the mechanisms by which normal cells respond to DNA damage and the consequences of these responses.
understanding the mechanisms by which cells respond to DNA damaging agents, and the consequences of these responses for cancer development and progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the senescence associated-secretory phenotype (SASPs) is a novel, important, and potentially exploitable aspect of senescence.
SASP factors secreted by genotoxic stress induced cells can promote epithelial mesenchymal transition and invasion in a paracrine manner, which can promote the malignant transformation of cells.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SASPs induced by DNA damage are a major mechanism by which senescence suppress cancer by altering the microenvironment.
senescent cells release inflammatory mediators that promote the development of cancer.
the SASPs are a novel mechanism by which p 53 and oncogenic R 53 act to regulate the tissue microenvironment, with implications for cancer development.
The main takeaway from our work is that
senescent cells can have profound effects on their tissue microenvironments by secreting a wide variety of factors that are associated with inflammation and cancer.
senescent cells are not simply a passive bystander in the process of tumorigenesis.
cells undergoing senescence secrete a complex array of cytokines, proteases, growth factors, and other molecules.
